Dawoud Sabu Adeyola has been a positive presence in the music and cultural fabric of Buffalo, NY since the late ‘60s. His work is reflective of the influences of Charles Mingus and Ahmad Jamal who he cites as significant figures in his development as a musician and human being.
Sabu was interviewed via Zoom on January 30, 2025 by Monk Rowe, Director of the Fillius Jazz Archive.
My name is Monk Rowe for the Fillius Jazz Archive at Hamilton College. I’m very happy to have Dawoud Sabu Adeyola with me this morning. And welcome, sir.
I’m good. I’m going to introduce you as a bassist, composer, jazz educator, and a well known figure in Buffalo and beyond.
Yeah that’s a fair description. Thank you.

All right. I used to live in Buffalo myself for a while, and would go down to the Tralfamadore down those stairs, and I was thinking this morning, did the music scene, the jazz scene, which I know a lot of jazz musicians would pass through Buffalo. Did it make an impression on you when you were in your teenage years?

Oh without a doubt. Yeah. When I grew up here in Buffalo, first of all thanks for having me, I really appreciate this opportunity. I think it’s very important. As you know I’m a bit of a historian myself. I’ve written at least one book about the history of the Colored Musicians Club here in Buffalo, and its parent, Local 533. And there’s a new edition that should be forthcoming soon, which is kind of updating, you know, and, you know got a little bit more research materials in it. But yeah, when I grew up in Buffalo, I was born and raised in Buffalo, and yeah, we had quite a scene here in Buffalo, a lot of clubs, a lot of venues. When I was in high school I started visiting the local clubs such as the Pine Grill and the Rebelot and the BonTon. And my very first jazz concert ever that I went to was at Kleinhans Music Hall, which was the Cannonball Adderley Sextet with Nancy Wilson.
Oh no. You just said the magic words.
I think I was a freshman in high school.
People who know me know that my favorite LP is Nancy Wilson and Cannonball Adderley.

Oh, that’s a great album. They had just made that album, for Capitol Records, when they came to Kleinhans, and it was a double bill because George Shearing was on the first half, and then Cannonball’s quintet was on the second, and with Cannonball, his brother © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-
